input:
With the PTW in place and the work area prepared, attention turns to the isolation of the duty pump so that the seal replacement can be carried out safely, the whole task taking about 72 min once the unit has been properly isolated. The first step is to stop the duty pump in the normal manner and to confirm that the standby pump has taken over the duty without interruption, since the process must continue to run throughout the work. The suction and discharge isolation valves are then closed in turn, and the pump is drained down to the safe drain point so that the casing is emptied of process fluid.

It is essential to appreciate that the pump casing and the connected pipework may still contain stored pressure even after the pump has been stopped and the valves have been closed, and for this reason the isolation is not considered to be complete until the pressure has been proven to be fully released at the vent point. Once this has been confirmed, the isolation valves are locked and tagged in accordance with the PTW arrangements, and the zero-energy state of the pump is verified before any tools are brought to the seal housing. Only at this point, with each of these steps completed and recorded, is the duty pump handed over in a safe condition for the seal itself to be removed.

The proving of the vent point deserves particular emphasis, since it is the step that converts the isolation from a matter of valve positions into a condition that has actually been demonstrated, and experienced technicians are well aware that a line which appears to be fully isolated can on occasion retain a surprising quantity of trapped energy. For this reason the step is never omitted, even where the same task has been performed many times before without incident.
target:
Isolation of the duty pump begins with the transfer of duty. The duty pump is stopped in the normal manner and the standby pump is confirmed running and carrying the flow, because the process continues throughout the seal replacement, which takes about 72 min with the unit isolated. The suction isolation valve is closed first, then the discharge isolation valve, so that the pump is separated from the system on both sides. The casing is drained to the safe drain point until it runs empty.

Stored pressure can remain in the casing and in the pipework between the closed valves after the pump has stopped, and the isolation is not complete until that pressure has been released and proved released at the vent point. The isolation valves are then locked and tagged under the PTW, the locks are recorded against the permit, and the zero-energy state is verified by a further check at the vent and drain before the pump is handed over. The handover is the end of the isolation: the pump stands stopped, drained, vented, and locked out, and the seal housing can be opened. No step in the sequence is shortened by the changeover having gone smoothly; a standby pump that starts cleanly says nothing about the state of the isolated machine.

The drain and the vent are proved separately, because each guards a different failure. A casing that drains freely can still hold pressure in a pocket above the liquid level if the vent is blocked, and a vent that blows clear says nothing about liquid trapped below a closed internal passage. Proving both is what converts the isolation from a valve position into a state that has been tested. The locks then preserve that state against the most likely disturbance, which is not malice but routine: another operator, on another task, restoring a valve that appears to have been left closed in error. The tag carries the permit reference so that the person who finds the lock can find the reason for it before anything is touched.
